subject: lion
pitch: A proud old lion resting with his head held high. A huge shaggy mane fading from golden blond at the face to dark chocolate at the edges, a tawny body with a pale cream belly and muzzle, amber eyes, a broad black nose, a scar across one eyebrow, big padded paws and a long tail ending in a dark tuft.
reasoning:
I'm planning out a rigged lion module in a resting sphinx pose, with front legs extended forward and hind legs folded beneath, keeping the joint structure manageable rather than overly complex.

I'm sketching the skeleton hierarchy: hip root, a spine chain curving up to the shoulders, a neck chain continuing to the head, and then jaw and other head joints attached off that chain using the library's chain and joint helpers for positioning and parenting.

For the body mesh, I'm sweeping a shape along the spine chain to build an elliptical torso that deepens toward the chest, with radius values tapering from rear to front, then applying a countershaded tawny-to-cream coloring.

I'm adjusting the spine's vertical positioning so the belly sits closer to the ground, lowering the centerline and tuning the ellipse radius so a lying lion's underside rests near the floor rather than floating above it.

Then I'm building the neck as a curve of points rising from the shoulder toward the head, with the neck radius tapering slightly since it'll mostly be hidden by the mane. For the head, I'm placing it at the end of the neck and sketching out a skull shape using a scaled sphere positioned relative to the head's local coordinate frame, thinking through how the forward offset and axis scaling should work for the mesh.

Working out muzzle geometry...

Skipping the lip detailing for simplicity, I'm moving to the eyes: amber spheres with dark pupils positioned using head-local coordinates, accounting for left/right orientation, placed at a consistent forward/up offset with small radius, plus a pupil dot on front and a brow shape above.

Now I'm adding a scar detail across one eyebrow using a thin pale-pink rod positioned on the left eye side, estimating head-local coordinates that trace from above the eye down to below it, though I need to make sure it sits properly on the skull surface rather than floating since the skull is an ellipsoid shape with specific radii.

Checking whether the eye coordinates actually land on the skull ellipsoid surface rather than inside it — the math shows the current placement is too far inward, so instead I'll use a surface-hit function that casts around the skull shape by azimuth and elevation to find the true surface point, guarding against null results, then attach the eye sphere there.

Now I'm thinking through the mane: it needs to surround and sit behind the head without covering the face. I'm planning to build it from scattered tuft-textured cards layered over a lobed core volume, with a golden-to-chocolate color gradient based on distance from the face, centered roughly behind the neck and flattened into shape.

Writing color gradient function...

I'll plan the mane as tufted spike-shapes rather than plain geometry—using flame-shaped greyscale card textures tinted by the paint color, built around a core sphere scaled up and painted with the mane color.

For positioning, I'm placing the main mane as an ellipsoid near the back of the neck/head, plus smaller chest and shoulder mane ellipsoids, making sure the skull and muzzle poke forward through the mane's front radius so the face emerges naturally rather than being buried.

Setting the ring cards to lean back around the face with a gold tone near the muzzle, then scattering mane cards across the mane core surface with varied size, lean, and bend to flow back and down, filtering out hits too close to the face.

I'm also adding a mane stripe under the chest, computing mane color by distance from the face for darker edges, and planning round ears next.

I'll add 4 whisker dots per side on the muzzle with small dark brown spots, placed at varying azimuth and elevation offsets near the nose. Now moving to the legs: for a lying sphinx pose, I'm chaining the front leg joints from shoulder down to elbow, with the upper arm angling down-back toward the ground and the forearm extending forward along the ground to the paw.

I need to be careful with world coordinates here—world +X corresponds to left, so I'll name sides based on the sign of x directly rather than relying on local model orientation, keeping it consistent with the world frame. Then I'm sweeping tubes along each leg chain with tapering radii, thicker at the shoulder and narrowing toward the paw, defining three segments (shoulder-elbow, elbow-wrist, wrist-tip) across four named joints.

Still adjusting leg geometry...

Still working out paw colors and joint positions...

I'm adjusting the hind leg geometry since the knee-hock-toe chain creates too sharp a zigzag; I'm tapering the radii from thigh to foot and repositioning the hock and toe so the foot sits more naturally in line with the shin instead of bending back 160 degrees.

Setting up the hind leg with a rigid skin sweep to avoid deformation weirdness, using a four-point chain from hip to toe with tapering radii, plus a haunch ellipsoid and paw shape for the lion's hindquarters.

Now I'm working out the tail curve, placing it as a chain from the rump curling to one side along the ground with decreasing radius toward a tuft at the tip, adjusting the point positions to get the right overall length.

Shaping the tuft as a tapered rod with varying radii along a straight path for a teardrop profile, then considering scattering small dark cards over it for texture, and checking how to pull the tangent direction from the tail's endpoint.

I'm figuring out the tail's end position and direction so the tuft points forward-left naturally, blending a tawny-to-dark countershaded gradient so the tuft overlaps hide any seam. For the body, I'm planning a sweep with radii that vary by parameter to shape the haunch and cream belly via countershading.

Now I'm setting up the spine chain points from hips to shoulders, extending the rear further back so the rump has room to form a rounded dome, and parenting the hip joints to keep the hind legs anchored correctly. I need to recheck the radius values though, since the current numbers would place the belly below ground level instead of resting low but clear.

Still tuning radii and shift values...

Checking that the sink keeps the paws touching y=0 within tolerance, and deciding to skip extra shoulder bulges since the mane will cover them. Now I'm sketching the neck sweep with its own radii and chain of points leading up toward where the head joint sits.

Shifting the head joint and skull center forward, then placing the mane ellipsoid so it wraps around the skull sides—checking whether the cheek stays just outside the mane surface at the widest point or pokes through slightly.

Checking that eyes positioned at the 35-degree azimuth sit outside the mane boundary so they stay visible, then nudging the main mane ellipsoid back along z. I'm also laying out the chest and shoulder mane ellipsoids to build volume below the head, and thinking about how to break up the mane's smooth ellipsoid edges so it reads as shaggy rather than a solid blob.

Setting up low-poly tuft cards for the mane, scattered across the surface parts and tinted by distance from a reference point, plus cheek ruff cards arranged in a ring. Defining the lion's color palette (tawny, cream, gold, chocolate) as hex-to-RGB arrays for use in the shaders, and sketching an SVG path for a tapering tuft lock shape.

Setting up the color blend for the mane paint, shifting gold to amber-brown to chocolate based on the threshold value, then defining a darker tuft color for the tail.

For the eyes, I'm placing an amber sphere with a dark pupil embedded via a stick-seated hit point, offsetting the pupil slightly outward along the normal. I'm considering whether to add eyeliner rings or brow ridges for more detail but may skip the heavier lid geometry to keep things simple.

Now I'm building the brow ridge as a flattened, scaled sphere oriented along the surface normal, colored tawny-gold, and adding a scar on the left eye side—a rod connecting two hit points near the brow with a slight outward offset, accounting for how the chord between curved points on the skull dips inward relative to the surface.

Just using skull.at as the default center for the surface call makes sense without needing extra args. I'm working out azimuth convention (0=+Z, 90=+X) for eye placement with symmetric offsets, and noting the skull ellipsoid relies on scaled sphere geometry. For the nose, I'm sticking a flattened, scaled sphere onto the muzzle front at low elevation to form a black wedge shape.

Now I'm placing the bridge and muzzle ellipsoids with specific forward/down offsets and scales, checking that the muzzle tip aligns near 0.36 forward matching the nose hit point, and verifying the bridge sits slightly above the muzzle's top edge. Then I'm setting up the jaw joint and aim points with their own forward/down offsets and an ellipsoid shape in cream tone.

I'm adjusting the muzzle's vertical scale and center so its lower edge clears the jaw's upper edge, keeping the mouth closed naturally, then adding a thin dark ellipsoid along the mouth line for a subtle closed-mouth seam.

Now I'm setting up a ring of fur card elements around the head to form cheek tufts and a ruff—using a radial ring positioned along the head's forward axis, with 16 cards at radius 0.19, leaning back at roughly 70 degrees so their faces orient outward and backward along the skull.

I'm checking the ring's placement relative to the mane geometry: at a forward offset of 0.05 the radius exceeds the skull width, leaving the cards floating in air past the mane's front edge, so I'm testing a slightly pulled-back position (around z=0.87) where the mane's elliptical cross-section is wide enough to anchor the card roots properly.

I'm tuning the gold-to-chocolate color gradient along the mane cards using a smoothstep based on distance from the face point, then moving on to place small tawny ear spheres near the top of the skull, acknowledging they may get partially hidden behind the mane cards but deciding that's acceptable.

I'm deciding to skip adding extra elbow fringe and fur texture cards for now, and instead focusing on the forepaws -- adding toe spheres offset along the paw ellipsoid to give each front paw a set of distinct toes.

Now I'm checking which bone to anchor the paw tip to, making sure the leg chain's tip joint is used rather than a null reference, and roughing out the elbow and upper-arm proportions so they sit naturally under the shoulder before the mane and body fur cover them.

Setting up the imports and body coloring with mottled countershading, then starting the spine chain by placing the hip joint and building a catmull-rom spline through the body points...

Still writing the chain hierarchy...

Then I'm setting up the head joint attached to the neck's endpoint, orienting it forward, and starting the loop for building the left and right foreleg limbs symmetrically.

Building foreleg chains with tapered radii...

Now checking the hind leg joint placement — hip, knee, hock, toe — and I'm noticing the shin and foot segments would collapse onto the same line at the hock, so I need to offset the toe laterally to avoid overlapping geometry.

I'll shift the shin outward (knee x .3, hock x .29) with the foot tucked slightly inward (toe x .2), and use straight polyline segments instead of catmull smoothing for the sharp hock fold since smoothing would loop oddly there. The haunch ellipsoid covers the joint seam, so minor overlap is fine, and I'll position it at the hip with tawny coloring to blend into the body.

Working out the hind paw proportions, I'm placing the tail root behind the rump cap and defining a curved chain of points sweeping down and back for the tail shape, tapering the radii toward the tip. For the tail tuft, I'm calculating the endpoint position and tangent direction to offset a small sweep shape outward along the tail's end direction.

Scattering dark cards onto the tuft sweep for texture, then setting up similar card scattering for the mane, rooted on the neck bone's last joint with leaning and bending variation. I'm also sketching how painted spheres will form the mane's core shapes along the neck.

Now I'm planning several mane lumps—main mass, chest, shoulder, and cheek clusters—each with position and radius variants, and considering how scatter counts and minimum distances will keep the hits from clumping too densely while still filtering for front-facing coverage near the face.

Confirming that scatter works across nested part arrays, I then sketch the nose geometry as a small cream sphere offset forward and down from the head, scaled to a flattened shape, with a surface wrap defined for placing details around it.

For whiskers, I'm placing dot markers at angled offsets around the nose surface using small dark spheres, guarding against null hit results with a helper.

Now I'm defining the skull part as a gold-faced sphere offset forward from the head and scaled into an elongated shape, using a plain hex color for the face rather than a gradient. I write a hitAt helper that wraps the surface-around-point lookup and throws if no hit is found, then use it to place eyes and a brow stick geometry at angled offsets with embed and scale options, finishing with the meta export for the whole model.

I'm now plotting a scar as a swept catmull-rom curve crossing diagonally over the brow and eye region, computing the angular offsets so it clears the raised brow geometry, and setting up the sweep with a small radius, rounded caps, and explicit bone binding to the head frame.

Checking the ground contact points next: forepaw and hind paw ellipsoid centers and radii line up correctly at zero, tail tuft looks fine, and I still need to finalize the toe loops before writing everything out.
